title: Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures
shortTitle: Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures
summary: SQL Stored Procedures is the database form of persistence under the Server Software Component parent. A stored procedure is a named block of database code that users call by name, and database engines store these blocks inside system catalog tables. Because the engine loads and runs them on request, a procedure that an administrator does not expect becomes durable code execution inside the database service. Adversaries either create their own procedure or modify an existing one, then arrange for it to run automatically, for example when the instance starts. Rewriting the procedure achieves survival across restarts, while invocation from a legitimate application account blends the activity into ordinary database traffic. Impact escalates when the engine offers host-level features: Microsoft SQL Server can execute operating system commands through xp_cmdshell when that option is enabled, and its common language runtime integration lets procedures call external code libraries that run arbitrary logic. Detection therefore centres on the database audit trail and the configuration of the engine itself: new or altered procedure definitions in the system catalog, changes to the startup procedure setting, changes to xp_cmdshell or runtime integration options, and procedure executions callable only from privileged or network-exposed accounts.

beginner.definition: A stored procedure is a piece of database code that is saved with a name and can be called again later, a bit like a saved recipe. This technique describes an attacker adding or changing a saved recipe so that the database runs their hidden instructions. The database then becomes a quiet place for the attacker to live and to run commands.
beginner.whyItMatters: Databases sit at the centre of most business records, so code that runs inside a database can read or change almost anything. A saved procedure survives restarts, updates and password changes, which makes it far more reliable for an attacker than a program they have to re-upload. On Microsoft SQL Server, extra features can let saved database code run commands on the operating system itself, turning a data problem into a whole-server problem. Many teams only review the database for performance and backup issues, so hidden code can stay in place for a long time.
howItWorks: The attacker gains a database account with enough rights, often a stolen administrator login.
They create a new stored procedure, or alter an existing one, and save it in the database.
Database systems keep saved procedures in their own system tables, so the code is stored quietly.
The attacker may turn on extra features so the saved code can run commands on the operating system.
The procedure may be attached to a start-up event so it runs again every time the database restarts.
Normal applications still use the database, and the hidden procedure runs under a trusted account.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital pharmacy with a printed standard recipe pinned to the wall, which any staff member follows when preparing a common medicine. Someone quietly changes that pinned card so it also adds an extra ingredient nobody ordered. Everyone keeps following the same recipe as before, and the change is only noticed if somebody actually reads the card and compares it with the original.
takeaways: Review saved database code, not just who has database passwords.
Watch for new procedures and for changes to start-up or command execution settings.
Database audit records that name the calling account are your best evidence.

objectives: Define what a stored procedure is and how a database keeps it between restarts.
Explain how a modified procedure survives restarts and updates inside a database service.
Describe the engine settings that let database code run operating system commands.
Identify the audit records that show a procedure was created, changed or executed.
Compare an unexpected stored procedure change against normal release and change control.
